messages.author: d7f310b4072e9be9
messages.subject: transect length and encounter rate
parts:
Hi All,
I have two related questions:
1) Is there a calculation or rule of thumb to optimize transect length for minimal encounter rate variance?
I understand numerous transects are desirable as these are the essential sampling unit when inference is to be extrapolated to the larger study area.
However, 2) What (if any) harm or trade off is there from a study design having many transects with zero encounters versus fewer transects with low encounter rate variance?
Thanks!
G
M

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] transect length and encounter rate
parts:
Hi Derek,

Regarding your first question, I don't think you can change transect length to obtain a minimal encounter rate variance. The encounter rate variance (which represents the variance in number of detections as a function of units of effort) is a function of the degree of clustering of the animal population you are trying to survey, so it is not something that you can control. Having said that, placing transects perpendicular to gradients of density will help, because you will tend to make counts more similar across transects.
Regarding the second, there is absolutely no problem in having many transects without observations. For the same amount of total effort, the larger the number of transects the better, for at least 3 reasons: (1) better spatial coverage; (2) better estimates of encounter rate variance and (3) the more likely it is that the underlying assumptions about animal distribution within the covered strips are valid (uniform in lines and triangular for points, which is ensured by design given the random placement of transects in the study area). Of course that might come at a logistic cost, but that is a cost to weight against the above mentioned benefits.
Hope this helps,
Tiago

If I understand correctly, you suggest segmenting it randomly and analyzing it as many short transects.
For curiosity's sake, can you give me an idea of how my estimates of density and encounter rate would vary when these data are analyzed as 1 vs. many transects?
Thanks,
Derek

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] transect length and encounter rate
parts:
Hi Derek,

You have a problem, because your situation was not what I was expecting. My suggestions were from a survey design point of view, before data collection. I am NOT suggesting  "segmenting it randomly and analysing it as many short transects", in fact I advise you against that procedure.

If you only have one transect of 40 km, you can't simply cut it into 1000 transects of 40 meters and off you go. That is akin to pseudoreplication, because you treat each segment as an independent sampling unit, when they are not. The consequences are:
1. The point estimates will remain exactly the same one way or the other
2. The variance will be artificially decreased as you increase the number of transects - that you can change your variance estimates depending on an arbitrary choice of segment number/lengths should tell you there's something not adequate about it.

So, all in all, you do not have many transects, you have just one, and there's no analysis that will get you out of that. At best you might obtain the variance based on assumptions (see the Distance manual for possible options, including a Poisson or overdispersed Poisson assumption), but that has it's downsides.

Further, after considering that, if you have transects along roads you might have a problem, because the underlying assumption that transects have been placed at random with respect to the animals is violated, and if the animals do respond to roads, you could considerably underestimate or overestimate density.

Sorry for the promotion of my own work, but take a look at this paper for why that is the case and a possible solution (if you happen to have information about the distribution of animals with respect to the road from an independent source):

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Bispo, R. & Howland, B. 2013 Accounting for animal density gradients using independent information in distance sampling surveys Statistical Methods and Applications 22: 67-80

Best

T

Best wishes,
Derek

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] transect length and encounter rate
parts:
Hi Derek, Pierre, list

In my opinion, and road issues aside, provided that the one transect covers adequately the entire area one wants to make inferences for, then having a single transect with say 100 km, that one subdivides into 100 1 km segments, and then analyses every other one (so 50 transects), is not breaking any "statistical" rules. Probably someone will add to the discussion and tell me otherwise.

Now this is not me recommending that process, because the truth is that this is only reasonable if the coverage of the survey area is adequate, where adequate here is a vague concept, and you are much better off starting with a sensible survey design for making the inferences that you are interested in making. Also, it seems ineffective for logistical reasons, as you are having to travel across all the off effort areas.

Coming down to Pierre's point, I believe even the correlation that is induced because the segments were originally along "the same transect" is, to some extent, not an issue. Just in the same way as if one placed a design like the one below with just the blue lines considered on effort and the orange lines off effort, each transect would be considered an independent sampling unit, independently of them being along several different transects originally - we know that spatial autocorrelation will be present to a larger or smaller degree depending on the "clumpiness" of the population, but in conventional distance sampling we simply treat the transects as independent sampling units (that is e.g. why under a bootstrap it is recommended that you bootstrap lines, not detections).

See the study area below as an example, where effectively a single transect was conducted. You could obtain a density estimate from the blue lines as (much smaller) transects, and a robust variance around it. But then...by the same token, you could get one from the orange transects. How would you then combine the two? You can imagine this example being extended to having many subsets of transects. Depending on having or not to pool data for the detection function across subsets, these might correspond to independent or correlated density estimates, and hence how one would combine these to obtain the density estimate of interest might not be straightforward.

To conclude, my final advice is, perhaps not surprisingly... ignore all the above as it's possibly just causing confusion and opening a can of worms. Also because if you do have the entire area of inference covered, then the variance estimates from usual Distance sampling estimators are less than ideal, since they assume that you are covering a subset of a larger region such that finite correction factors are not used. But I felt I had to answer given Pierre's prompt. So: Plan your survey to have many lines, perpendicular to potential existing density gradients for the species of interest.

cheers,

T

PS - 
As an aside, if anyone out there actually has:
1. a single transect
2. covering the entire survey area they want to make inferences for
3. ideally not from roads or any other linear structure potentially promoting a density gradient)
please contact me off the list. I'd like, (time permitting!) to explore some ideas under that setting.


Sem vírus. www.avast.com

If you only have one transect of 40 km, you can't simply cut it into 1000 transects of 40 meters and off you go. That is akin to pseudoreplication, because you treat each segment as an independent sampling unit, when they are not. The consequences are:

1. The point estimates will remain exactly the same one way or the other

2. The variance will be artificially decreased as you increase the number of transects - that you can change your variance estimates depending on an arbitrary choice of segment number/lengths should tell you there's something not adequate about it.

 

So, all in all, you do not have many transects, you have just one, and there's no analysis that will get you out of that. At best you might obtain the variance based on assumptions (see the Distance manual for possible options, including a Poisson or overdispersed Poisson assumption), but that has it's downsides.

 

Further, after considering that, if you have transects along roads you might have a problem, because the underlying assumption that transects have been placed at random with respect to the animals is violated, and if the animals do respond to roads, you could considerably underestimate or overestimate density.

 

Sorry for the promotion of my own work, but take a look at this paper for why that is the case and a possible solution (if you happen to have information about the distribution of animals with respect to the road from an independent source):

 

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Bispo, R. & Howland, B. 2013 Accounting for animal density gradients using independent information in distance sampling surveys Statistical Methods and Applications 22: 67-80

 

Best

 

T

To get more into the details, I don't have random systematic transects.

If I understand correctly, you suggest segmenting it randomly and analyzing it as many short transects.

On Monday, November 20, 2017 at 10:49:42 AM UTC+1, Tiago Marques wrote:

Hi Derek,

 

Regarding your first question, I don't think you can change transect length to obtain a minimal encounter rate variance. The encounter rate variance (which represents the variance in number of detections as a function of units of effort) is a function of the degree of clustering of the animal population you are trying to survey, so it is not something that you can control. Having said that, placing transects perpendicular to gradients of density will help, because you will tend to make counts more similar across transects.

Regarding the second, there is absolutely no problem in having many transects without observations. For the same amount of total effort, the larger the number of transects the better, for at least 3 reasons: (1) better spatial coverage; (2) better estimates of encounter rate variance and (3) the more likely it is that the underlying assumptions about animal distribution within the covered strips are valid (uniform in lines and triangular for points, which is ensured by design given the random placement of transects in the study area). Of course that might come at a logistic cost, but that is a cost to weight against the above mentioned benefits.

Hope this helps,

Tiago

parts:
To echo some of Tiago's sentiments:

There will be plenty of challenges to any biological survey: poor weather, equipment malfunction, tiring work, difficult measurements.  There will be no shortage of actors that will conspire to foil your intention of making defensible inferences about the population you are studying.  These difficulties will arise regardless of whether the survey design is good or poor.  Design is a feature of the survey over which the investigator has the greatest control.

A sensible approach is to *start* with a competent survey design.  If the design is poor, these other events outside investigator control cannot improve the inferences drawn.
On 23/11/2017 15:04, Tiago Marques wrote:

Hi Derek, Pierre, list

In my opinion, and road issues aside, provided that the one transect covers adequately the entire area one wants to make inferences for, then having a single transect with say 100 km, that one subdivides into 100 1 km segments, and then analyses every other one (so 50 transects), is not breaking any "statistical" rules. Probably someone will add to the discussion and tell me otherwise.

Now this is not me recommending that process, because the truth is that this is only reasonable if the coverage of the survey area is adequate, where adequate here is a vague concept, and you are much better off starting with a sensible survey design for making the inferences that you are interested in making. Also, it seems ineffective for logistical reasons, as you are having to travel across all the off effort areas.

Coming down to Pierre's point, I believe even the correlation that is induced because the segments were originally along "the same transect" is, to some extent, not an issue. Just in the same way as if one placed a design like the one below with just the blue lines considered on effort and the orange lines off effort, each transect would be considered an independent sampling unit, independently of them being along several different transects originally - we know that spatial autocorrelation will be present to a larger or smaller degree depending on the "clumpiness" of the population, but in conventional distance sampling we simply treat the transects as independent sampling units (that is e.g. why under a bootstrap it is recommended that you bootstrap lines, not detections).

See the study area below as an example, where effectively a single transect was conducted. You could obtain a density estimate from the blue lines as (much smaller) transects, and a robust variance around it. But then...by the same token, you could get one from the orange transects. How would you then combine the two? You can imagine this example being extended to having many subsets of transects. Depending on having or not to pool data for the detection function across subsets, these might correspond to independent or correlated density estimates, and hence how one would combine these to obtain the density estimate of interest might not be straightforward.

To conclude, my final advice is, perhaps not surprisingly... ignore all the above as it's possibly just causing confusion and opening a can of worms. Also because if you do have the entire area of inference covered, then the variance estimates from usual Distance sampling estimators are less than ideal, since they assume that you are covering a subset of a larger region such that finite correction factors are not used. But I felt I had to answer given Pierre's prompt. So: Plan your survey to have many lines, perpendicular to potential existing density gradients for the species of interest.

cheers,

T

PS - 
As an aside, if anyone out there actually has:
1. a single transect
2. covering the entire survey area they want to make inferences for
3. ideally not from roads or any other linear structure potentially promoting a density gradient)
please contact me off the list. I'd like, (time permitting!) to explore some ideas under that setting.


Sem vírus. www.avast.com
